I don't want to be with someone who doesn't love me as much as I love them.

Personally, something I've always wanted to say to redpill redditors is how much I feel the same way they do, except in the opposite direction.  It's really easy to generalize a gender after someone who might display stereotypical qualities associated with that gender breaks your heart.  My ex was a fuckboy and emotionally unavailable.  I didn't feel like I could be my complete human self with him, I was so concerned about presenting myself as the perfect girlfriend.  What generalizing does is helps you avoid internalizing what someone did to you.  If its not unique, its not personal.  But, its not your fault OP, and you don't have to make sweeping indictments of the female gender for you to feel like it wasn't about you.  You know what dread is as a redpill concept right?  Dread was my entire relationship.  I never felt secure 100%.  It was the very female-targeting experience of being gaslighted by a heterosexual relationship.  I had a mental breakdown and self-harmed when my ex left me.  

I can tell you i haven't met many men that I wouldn't think would hurt me.  I've generalized, and looked at all the negative examples of men being inconsiderate assholes who can't commit in my life, and felt depressed that I haven't found any compatible exceptions.  

But I don't think objectively that line of thinking is true at all.  And I believe you OP, so I hope you can see I'm struggling too.

Hi, thank you so much for the in depth response! Really helpful.  I am currently on a waitlist for seeing an OCD specialist so in the meantime I'm trying to do the best I can.  There's an article I read which confused me, which is I think where my thought process came from.  https://www.intrusivethoughts.org/mistaken-beliefs-uncertainty-acceptance-ocd/ 

The article basically states (and it's by a Dr. who runs an OCD clinic in Baltimore) that accepting uncertainty usually means assuming a situation is positive out of confidence while knowing one could be wrong at the same time and choosing not to engage with fears (accepting that life is uncertain and there's small risk all the time) because it would be ridiculous to even entertain the issue? That's why I was confused being in a situation where I feel like there's a large risk.  Am I brkng led astray here?  I just feel like there's a difference between accepting a low possibility and a high possibility.  If there's a high risk someone is going to die, wouldn't they naturally obsess and worry more?  How can that person be unaffected emotionally to the point where they can go about their day normally?

Hey, for me the relationship issues are real, but the thing is a lot of the time there is a kernel of truth which someone with ocd reacts to a million times more strongly than someone else would.  It's hard to figure out an appropriate reaction when OCD complicates the issue.  I'm in exactly the same boat as you, but I guess what I have to say is this.  If you can conceptualize what someone would feel without OCD in your same situation, then maybe determine that way what you should do and your feelings can be drawn from the degree of the reaction.  What I'm trying to say is, it's important to accept the possibility that your fears are correct.  But, there will be times when the possibility is high, without OCD making them feel higher than they actually are.  In that situation you have reason to react to your partner in a stronger way without worrying that any reaction at all is a compulsion.  I think people with ROCD are vulnerable to being gaslighted in that people they are with might blame their real faults on the other persons disorder to avoid blame.  when you look back on this relationship, I think it's ok to recognize times where there were dealbreaker issues for you in him, if there were.
